title: Detecting Changes in XML Documents
research_question: How can two versions of a large XML document be compared efficiently to recover node correspondence and a compact edit description that includes subtree moves as well as insertions, deletions, and updates?
methodology: The paper develops an XML-tree differencing algorithm, BULD, that first establishes node correspondences and then constructs a delta between the old and new documents. It exploits XML ID attributes when available, computes signatures and weights for subtrees, matches large identical subtrees, and propagates matches bottom-up and lazily downward to find additional correspondences. The approach is evaluated with synthetically modified XML documents and a smaller collection of real web XML examples, measuring execution cost and the size or quality of generated deltas.

key_findings.finding: The algorithm explicitly models node correspondence between two document versions and can represent subtree moves in addition to insertions, deletions, and value updates.
XML ID attributes and subtree signatures provide strong anchors for preserving identity across versions, after which hierarchical propagation expands matches to related ancestors and descendants.

The implementation uses linear memory and exhibits approximately linear running-time behavior in the reported experiments, contrasting with earlier approaches characterized by the authors as quadratic.
On synthetically edited documents, the produced deltas are reported to remain reasonably close in size to the known edit scripts used to generate the modified versions.
On a small real-web sample, the XML-aware deltas have sizes comparable to conventional textual diff output while also encoding structural tree operations such as moves.
The method deliberately trades guaranteed global optimality for efficiency because optimal tree matching under the desired edit model is computationally difficult.

limitations: The heuristic matching algorithm does not guarantee a globally minimal or otherwise uniquely optimal delta.
Much of the empirical quality analysis uses synthetic mutations, whose distribution may not reproduce real editing behavior.
Only a small amount of real web XML data is presented because of space constraints.

The authors state that a fair comprehensive comparison with competing XML-diff systems would require substantially more experimentation because implementations, parsers, languages, and change distributions differ.
Delta byte size is only one possible quality criterion; the most useful correspondence can depend on downstream application semantics.
The method operates on XML tree structure and textual/attribute values rather than visual or multimodal document evidence.

There is no workbook-aware model of sheets, formulas, merged cells, row/column moves, or visual page regions, so applying it to revised spreadsheet provenance would require an additional domain-specific structural model.
raw_claims: The system compares two XML trees by identifying which nodes in the new tree correspond to nodes in the old tree.
Its delta language can express insertion, deletion, update, and movement of subtrees.
XML ID attributes are used as high-confidence correspondence anchors when the same identifiers occur in both versions.
The algorithm hashes subtree content so that identical subtrees can be recognized efficiently.
Large unchanged subtrees are matched before additional correspondences are propagated through the hierarchy.
The authors call the matching strategy Bottom-Up, Lazy-Down propagation.
The stated memory complexity is linear in document size.
Reported running cost grows almost linearly in the performance experiments.
Synthetic experiments apply controlled insertion, deletion, update, and move operations before attempting to recover a delta.
The authors note that producing an optimal change description is computationally hard and therefore use heuristic matching.
The real-document experiment is limited in scale and is not presented as a comprehensive benchmark against every XML differencing system.
